articles.title: Appropriations for Municipal Operating Budget
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will raise and appropriate, transfer and/or appropriate from available funds, the sum of $42,322,565 to defray the necessary expenses of the departments, offices and boards of the Town, exclusive of the Regional Schools' budgets, or take any other action relative thereto.

historicalVotes.title: Accessory Dwelling Unit bylaw amendment (Article 30)
historicalVotes.summary: To comply with the state Affordable Homes Act, Town removed owner-occupancy requirements, design criteria, and parking mandates for ADUs within half a mile of the South Town rail station, and grandfathered existing nonconforming ADUs.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: The ADU reform opened the door for the housing-flexibility articles that followed — like the 2026 renovation fix for nonconforming lots.

historicalVotes.title: FY2025 operating levy limit override — $6.6 million
historicalVotes.summary: Facing health-insurance and inflation costs, the town asked voters to permanently raise the tax limit by $6.6 million for schools and municipal government. It passed by just 37 votes out of more than 6,300 cast.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: The override reset the levy baseline for every budget article since — the reason FY27 municipal spending could grow a modest 3.05% without a new override.

historicalVotes.title: MBTA Communities Overlay District (Article 12)
historicalVotes.summary: Town Meeting ended the town's 75-year single-family-only zoning history by allowing multifamily housing by right near the South Town commuter-rail station, with 10 deed-restricted affordable units required per 100, in perpetuity.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: Every MBTA-overlay zoning debate at the 2026 meeting — including the affordability question town meeting declined to act on — builds on this decision.

historicalVotes.title: Wetherbee Woods conservation purchase (Article 1)
historicalVotes.summary: Town bought 33.11 wooded acres at 19 & 35 Wetherbee Street — described as the "Agricultural Gateway to the Town" — for $3.68 million using a state grant, CPA funds, CPA-backed borrowing, and a $100,000 gift from the Town Conservation Trust.
historicalVotes.tally: Passed by 2/3 voice vote (364 voters present)
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: The 46 Taylor Road purchase and the CPA package reuse this exact funding recipe: state money first, CPA second, private fundraising third, bonding last.

historicalVotes.title: $5.42M PFAS filtration at the Central Town Water Treatment Plant
historicalVotes.summary: Water District voters funded granular-activated-carbon PFAS treatment at the Central Town plant, with the South Town plant's larger retrofit approved by regulators to operate in May 2024.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: the town's water is funded and voted separately from town meeting — a useful reminder that some key local spending decisions happen outside Town Meeting entirely.

historicalVotes.title: Debt exclusion for the new Gates Elementary School
historicalVotes.summary: Voters approved excluding the bond costs of the town's share of the new Douglas–Gates elementary campus from Prop 2½ limits — one of two exclusions on that ballot, the other being the fire station.
historicalVotes.tally: 1,122 – 364 (fire station exclusion passed 1,169–315 the same day)
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: Pay-for-the-study, got-the-state-grant: the same playbook behind the $36.7M MSBA award and behind the 2026 Town Hall HVAC borrowing that leans on a $1M state grant.

historicalVotes.title: Debt exclusion for A-B Regional High School addition and remodel
historicalVotes.summary: A generation ago, town voters approved the town's share of a major expansion and remodel of the regional high school by a wide margin on an exclusion ballot.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: Two decades of school-facility investment ends up where the money is actually voted every year: the annual Article 8 regional school assessment.
